analysis.one_liner: Exempts drilling costs from the new minimum tax on billion-dollar corporations for oil, gas, and geothermal companies.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would carve oil and gas drilling costs out of the 15% corporate minimum tax, has sat in the Ways and Means Committee since January 2025 with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2022 Congress created a 15% minimum tax on very large corporations — those averaging over $1 billion in profits — calculated from the income companies report on their financial statements. This bill would let the biggest oil, gas, and geothermal drillers subtract intangible drilling and development costs, plus related depletion expenses, from that book income before the minimum tax applies [S2]. That means the largest fossil fuel producers would owe less under the minimum tax than other billion-dollar companies with the same reported profits [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders and executives of the largest oil and gas producers — the only companies the minimum tax applies to — would pay less tax when they spend on drilling and development. Geothermal drillers get the same treatment, though far fewer of them cross the $1 billion threshold. Lower tax bills could also give drillers more cash to reinvest in production.

how_it_helps.text: Corporations averaging over $1 billion in profits owe a 15% minimum tax on their adjusted financial statement income — the profit reported on their own financial statements — rather than regular taxable income [S2].

The bill lets these companies reduce that book income by intangible drilling and development costs for domestic oil, gas, or geothermal wells, and by related depletion expenses, before the minimum tax is calculated [S2][S3].
The change would apply to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Every dollar the largest drillers subtract from their book income under the minimum tax is revenue the government does not collect, which must be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing. The bill contains no offsetting revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill shrinks the base of the corporate minimum tax for one favored set of companies — large fossil fuel producers — while leaving the same tax fully in place for billion-dollar firms in every other industry, such as tech and pharma [S2][S3].
It reduces federal revenue with no pay-for, adding to deficits or forcing cuts or tax increases elsewhere [S2].
Any benefit to consumers through cheaper energy is indirect and unguaranteed: the tax cut flows to company shareholders first, and drilling decisions depend on oil prices, not tax treatment alone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefits go to a narrow group: the roughly few dozen corporations big enough to owe the minimum tax, most of them fossil fuel producers. The costs — lower federal revenue — are spread across everyone else. Supporters argue the change is fair because drilling costs are real business expenses, and the current minimum tax can tax income that hasn't been earned yet; but the bill grants that relief only to drilling companies, not to other capital-intensive billion-dollar businesses, which makes it hard to defend as anything but a targeted break.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and has had no hearing, markup, or floor action since.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Carey introduced the bill on January 23, 2025, with 33 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
The cosponsor list has since grown to 43 members — 40 Republicans and 3 Democrats — but the committee has taken no further action on the bill [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won anything yet. The bill has not advanced, so billion-dollar drillers have not received the tax break, and the Treasury has not lost the revenue it would forgo if the bill passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Mike Carey
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt drilling costs from the corporate minimum tax.

for.name: 3 of 217 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Reps. Vicente Gonzalez of Texas, Marc Veasey, Henry Cuellar)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining the Republican sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: Support is overwhelmingly Republican — 40 of 223 House Republicans versus 3 of 217 House Democrats — and no member or group has publicly opposed the bill, which has not been scheduled for any action.

industries.industry: Large oil and gas producers (billion-dollar corporations)
industries.note: These are the only companies the minimum tax reaches, and the bill lets them subtract drilling costs from their book income, lowering their minimum tax below what a tech or pharma company with identical reported profits would pay. Their gain comes directly out of federal revenue that other taxpayers must cover.

Geothermal well operators get the same deduction, though few are large enough to owe the minimum tax, so the practical benefit is small. Their interest in cheaper development roughly tracks the public's interest in more geothermal power, but the provision is bundled with a much larger oil and gas break.

industries.industry: Billion-dollar corporations outside energy (tech, pharma, banks)
industries.note: The minimum tax would stay fully in place for them while their fossil fuel competitors get a carve-out, putting them at a relative disadvantage — an argument opponents could raise if the bill ever moved.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action eight months after referral, the bill is unlikely to advance on its own; standalone tax bills rarely get floor time in the House. Its realistic path is as a provision folded into a larger tax package — Republicans have signaled interest in expanding the intangible drilling cost treatment in the 2025 tax debates — where it could pass without ever getting its own vote.
